html:
The Shuar, once widely called the Jívaro, are an Indigenous people of the Amazon rainforest on the eastern slopes of the Andes, in what is now southeastern Ecuador and northern Peru. Their language belongs to the small Jivaroan family, which they share with neighbours such as the Achuar.

Traditionally the Shuar lived in scattered households rather than villages, each a large oval house in a forest clearing. Women grew manioc and other crops in gardens; men hunted with blowguns and poison darts, and fished. Feuds and raids were part of life, and the Shuar were known as fierce defenders of their land. They are famous for the tsantsa, a shrunken head made from a slain enemy, part of a ritual meant to capture the enemy's soul.

Above all the Shuar kept their independence. The Inca under Huayna Capac tried to conquer them around 1500 and failed. The Spanish came for gold in the mid 1500s and built mining towns on their land; in 1599 the Shuar rose, destroyed the towns and drove the Spanish out. For about three centuries they stayed largely outside colonial control, which is why the map still shows them in 1815, long after Spanish America surrounded them.

Missions and settlers moved in from the late 1800s. In 1964 the Shuar founded one of the first Indigenous federations in South America to defend their land. Today more than 50,000 people speak Shuar. Many live by farming and hunting; some work in mining and timber. See also Shuar and Wampis and modern Ecuador.
